subject: 335D74632561E2EEA7E795D40A3FECE9
introduction: Shí‘ih tradition placed the hidden Twelfth Imam in two fabulous cities, Jábulqá and Jábarsá, at the eastern and western edges of the world, whence he would emerge with his companions. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá return to these cities as the standing example of a literal expectation that blinded a people: the divines searched for the Promised One in Jábulqá, and He was born in Shiraz. The Gospel of John records the same thing of Jesus’s contemporaries, who knew that the Messiah would come from no one knew where, or from Bethlehem, and so could not accept a man from Nazareth. The city “which hath foundations” in Hebrews and the new Jerusalem of the Apocalypse are unseen cities that the New Testament does not call illusions.
questions: Why is a hidden, marvellous origin so attractive an expectation? What does it protect believers from?
“Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” What would the modern form of that question be?
Hebrews praises looking for an unseen city. How is that different from the expectation the readings criticize?

outside.why: The Imams fixed His abode in the city of Jábulqá, a city no map shows. Neither shall they say, lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
A promised one invisible, with his servants, in a hidden city. The people of Jerusalem had the same expectation: when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is.
The Shí‘ihs deny because He did not come from where they looked. Shall Christ come out of Galilee? Hath not the scripture said that Christ cometh out of Bethlehem?
Jews too have awaited the Promised One from a concealed city. Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, come and see.
Whoever spoke otherwise was denounced. Is not this the carpenter’s son? is not his mother called Mary?
The divines, for all their knowledge, searched in Jábulqá. Where is the wise? where is the scribe? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?

“What hath become of those illusory cities?” Hebrews praises Abraham for seeking a city no map shows: he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God. What makes one unseen city an illusion and another the object of faith?
One who has “contrived a Jábulqá” leads the poor astray. They be blind leaders of the blind.

Some thought the source of this honey was in Jábulqá, others in the treasuries of heaven. John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven. How do the readings want such cities read: as places, or as figures for something that arrives among people?
